metadata.name: Radio Frequencies Reference
metadata.disclaimer: This information is for general reference only. Always comply with FCC regulations and local laws. Operating on certain frequencies may require proper licensing. Transmitting without a license where required is illegal.
sources: ARRL band plan (amateur simplex and calling frequencies)
Channel conventions not set by the FCC (CB 17, 19, 4, 13, 38; GMRS 20 with a 141.3 Hz tone; MURS Blue Dot and Green Dot) are labelled as conventions

HAM.title: HAM (Amateur Radio)
HAM.licenseInfo: ⚠️ LICENSE REQUIRED: You must have an FCC Amateur Radio License (Technician, General, or Amateur Extra) to transmit on amateur radio frequencies. A Technician license covers the VHF and UHF frequencies here; 29.600 MHz needs General or higher. Unlicensed transmission is illegal and subject to penalties.
HAM.description: Amateur Radio provides long-range communication capabilities. These are common nationwide frequencies accessible with appropriate licensing.

channels.name: 2m FM Simplex Calling
channels.notes: National simplex calling frequency. Make contact, then move to another simplex frequency

channels.name: 10m FM Simplex
channels.notes: 10-meter FM simplex frequency. General license or higher

CB.title: CB (Citizens Band)
CB.licenseInfo: ✓ NO LICENSE REQUIRED: CB radio can be used by anyone in the United States without a license. Maximum power: 4 watts AM, 12 watts PEP SSB. Channel 9 may only be used for emergencies and traveler assistance.
CB.description: Citizens Band radio operates on 40 channels between 26.965 and 27.405 MHz. Commonly used for short to medium-range communication.

channels.name: Channel 9
channels.notes: Emergencies and traveler assistance only (FCC rule)

channels.name: Channel 19
channels.notes: Highway and trucker channel, usually the busiest (convention)

channels.name: Channel 17
channels.notes: North/south highway traffic in some areas (convention)

GMRS.title: GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service)
GMRS.licenseInfo: ⚠️ LICENSE REQUIRED: GMRS requires an FCC license. The license covers you and your immediate family members. No exam is required; the fee is currently $35 for a 10-year license.
GMRS.description: GMRS operates on UHF frequencies with higher power limits than FRS, allowing for better range. Repeaters can extend coverage significantly.

FRS.title: FRS (Family Radio Service)
FRS.licenseInfo: ✓ NO LICENSE REQUIRED: FRS radios can be used without a license. Maximum power: 2 watts on channels 1-7 and 15-22, 0.5 watts on channels 8-14.
FRS.description: FRS is designed for short-range personal and family communication. All channels use FM mode. Range is typically 0.5-2 miles depending on terrain.

MURS.title: MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service)
MURS.licenseInfo: ✓ NO LICENSE REQUIRED: MURS can be used without a license. Maximum power: 2 watts. External antennas are permitted, unlike FRS, up to 60 feet above the ground or 20 feet above the structure they are on. Repeaters are not allowed.
MURS.description: MURS operates on VHF frequencies (151-154 MHz) providing better range than UHF FRS, especially in wooded areas. Five channels available.

channels.name: Channel 4 (Blue Dot)
channels.notes: Wider channel. "Blue Dot" is its business-radio nickname

channels.name: Channel 5 (Green Dot)
channels.notes: Wider channel. "Green Dot" is its business-radio nickname
